newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rival Lebed sees Yeltsin health troubles critical.
newsitem.headline: Rival Lebed sees Yeltsin health troubles critical.

text.p: Alexander Lebed, sacked as Russian President Boris Yeltsin's security adviser in October, sees the Kremlin leader's new bout of ill health as a key to his dream of revenge and ultimately taking power.
For Lebed, voted Russia's most popular politician seven months after he helped Yeltsin win re-election, the faster the president is deemed unable to continue in power, the better.

Lebed was blatantly quick to seize on the pneumonia which put Yeltsin, 65, back in bed just over two months after multiple heart bypass surgery. The 46-year-old former paratrooper denounced a "power vacuum" and resumed calls for the president to quit.
"The president is badly ill. It's a difficult age, he's had a difficult operation, a not entirely healthy way of life for the past 40 years. It doesn't leave much hope," Lebed told reporters.

"(Yeltsin) should offer his resignation. The president is in hospital, the prime minister is on holiday and people have not been paid and are not paid. No one has dealt with the economy or is dealing with the economy...
"Someone has to answer for that, someone has to rule,"
Twenty-four hours after Yeltsin was admitted to hospital, his doctors acknowledged he had pneumonia but said his condition was stable and predicted a rapid recovery.
Lebed, a former reserve general seen by many ordinary Russians as the only hope of rooting out endemic corruption, insisted that the country had been left "rudderless".

Opinion polls show him by far the most popular politician in Russia. One survey last month bestowed a Man of the Year award on him, far outpacing the ailing Yeltsin who was re-elected against long odds last July.
Should the president resign, stolid and scarcely popular Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin would take over for three months after which new elections would have to be held.
Last month, Lebed laid the foundation for his comeback by founding a political "third force" he hoped one day would win the allegiance of industry, intellectuals and the army.
Other rivals to Yeltsin eager to exploit any weakness, including Moscow's Mayor Yuri Luzhkov, could try to forge alliances to improve their chances.
Lebed was given the job of security chief for throwing the 15 percent electoral support he won last June to Yeltsin.
"I was born a winner. Sooner or later, victory will be mine," he said after his third-place finish behind Yeltsin and communist rival Gennady Zyuganov in last June's election.
He attributed his success not to siphoning off disaffected votes but "because I'm meaner".
But he crashed rapidly to earth as Yeltsin ruled against him in a bitter feud with Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov who accused Lebed of plotting a "creeping coup".
Yeltsin angrily announced Lebed's dismissal on television on October 17 as he was preparing for his heart bypass surgery.
During his brief stay inside Yeltsin's administration, Lebed's blunt approach won the admiration of Russian voters.
But his negotations ending the 18-month conflict in Chechnya launched by Yeltsin angered nationalists who saw it as a recipe for giving the region's separatists what they wanted.
Erratic statements generated enemies abroad -- disparaging remarks on U.S. Mormons and suggestions that Argentina was subject to recurrent coups.
Lebed was a career soldier who rose through the ranks of the paratroop forces and fought in the Soviet Afghan campaign.

His political career began in 1995 when he was removed as commander of Russia's 14th army in Moldova and resigned from active service. He had made his name in Moldova in 1992 by quelling fighting between government forces in the tiny state bordering Romania and Slav separatists from its Dnestr region.
